content:
The presence of Christ by the power of his word and the Holy Spirit

"Christ Jesus, who died, yes, who was raised from the dead, who is at the right hand of God, who indeed intercedes for us," is present in many ways to his Church: in his word, in his Church's prayer, "where two or three are gathered in my name," in the poor, the sick, and the imprisoned, in the sacraments of which he is the author, in the sacrifice of the Mass, and in the person of the minister. But "he is present … most especially in the Eucharistic species."

The mode of Christ's presence under the Eucharistic species is unique. It raises the Eucharist above all the sacraments as "the perfection of the spiritual life and the end to which all the sacraments tend." In the most blessed sacrament of the Eucharist "the body and blood, together with the soul and divinity, of our Lord Jesus Christ and, therefore, the whole Christ is truly, really, and substantially contained." "This presence is called 'real' - by which is not intended to exclude the other types of presence as if they could not be 'real' too, but because it is presence in the fullest sense: that is to say, it is a substantial presence by which Christ, God and man, makes himself wholly and entirely present."

It is by the conversion of the bread and wine into Christ's body and blood that Christ becomes present in this sacrament. the Church Fathers strongly affirmed the faith of the Church in the efficacy of the Word of Christ and of the action of the Holy Spirit to bring about this conversion. Thus St. John Chrysostom declares:

It is not man that causes the things offered to become the Body and Blood of Christ, but he who was crucified for us, Christ himself. the priest, in the role of Christ, pronounces these words, but their power and grace are God's. This is my body, he says. This word transforms the things offered.

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: This passage from the Catechism of the Catholic Church (§§1373–1375) expounds the doctrine of the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist, distinguishing the unique substantial presence in the Eucharistic species from Christ's other genuine modes of presence, and explaining how transubstantiation is effected by Christ's word and the Holy Spirit through the ministry of the priest.

[doctrinal | explicit]: Christ abides with his Church through multiple authentic modes of presence—in Sacred Scripture, communal prayer gathered in his name, the poor and suffering, the sacraments generally, the Eucharistic sacrifice, and the ordained minister—each constituting a real, though distinct, form of his ongoing communion with the faithful.

[doctrinal | explicit]: The Eucharist surpasses every other sacrament because Christ is present there "most especially," making the Blessed Sacrament the perfection of the spiritual life and the ultimate end toward which all other sacraments are ordered and directed.

[doctrinal | explicit]: In the consecrated Eucharistic species, the body, blood, soul, and divinity of Jesus Christ are truly, really, and substantially contained—the whole Christ, fully divine and fully human, present without reduction or partiality.

[doctrinal | explicit]: The Church's designation of Eucharistic presence as "real" does not diminish the authenticity of Christ's other modes of presence; rather, it affirms that this is presence in the fullest, most complete sense—a substantial indwelling by which Christ, God and man, gives himself wholly and entirely.

[doctrinal | explicit]: Christ's presence in the Eucharist is brought about through the substantial conversion of bread and wine into his body and blood—transubstantiation—so that his presence rests on a genuine ontological change in the offerings, not a mere addition or symbolic overlay upon unchanged elements.

[doctrinal/historical | explicit]: The efficacious power behind this conversion belongs to Christ himself and to the action of the Holy Spirit, a truth firmly attested by the Church Fathers, including St. John Chrysostom, who insists it is the crucified Christ—not any human agent—who transforms the offered gifts into his body and blood.

[doctrinal/moral | explicit]: The ordained priest speaks the words of consecration ("This is my body") in persona Christi, yet the transforming power and grace are entirely God's; the minister serves as instrument through whom Christ's own authoritative word accomplishes the Eucharistic change.
